newsitem.title: USA: NY Gov wants to spend more on health, environment.
newsitem.headline: NY Gov wants to spend more on health, environment.

text.p: New York State Gov. George Pataki, who admitted his initial budget hinged on getting Albany lawmakers to accept big cuts in Medicaid, proposed giving another $100 million to health-care providers.

In his revised budget, Pataki, who also was criticized for not spending enough under the $1.75 billion green bond approved by voters in November, called for doubling the amount that will be spent to $1 billion through 2002.
The additional aid for healthcare providers aims to help them make the transition to the deregulated arena, which forces them to negotiate rates with managed care companies.
Pataki made his proposed welfare program a bit more generous, asking for $2.5 million to aid legal immigrants who no longer are eligible for Supplemental Security Income.

Localities would continue to get a 50 percent reimbursement for all welfare programs eligible under the new Safety Net plan Pataki proposed. Another $5 million will be spent on a computer system for child welfare.

The governor has sought to satisfy New York City's demand that it get a fair share of a school tax relief program by including cooperative apartments--the vast majority of which are in the city--in the $3.4 billion program that will be phased in over five years. And moving to address the concerns of parents, Pataki went ahead with a $2 million plan for charter schools, clearing the way for the state to get federal funds for this initiative.
The governor also added $3.8 million for high technology initiatives, and $2.5 million of a $12 million program for the State Museum and State Archives.

In prepared remarks, he said: "Among other important provisions, my proposal will provide additional tax relief, help legal immigrants become citizens and continue the sweeping reforms to the welfare system intitiated two years ago."

The impact on the General Fund of all the proposed changes is $140 million, which is offset by $85 million in more revenues and $55 million in lower spending, which mainly will come from projected drops in welfare caseloads.
Total receipts in fiscal 1998 now are expected to be $63 million higher than when the preliminary budget was drafted in late January, according to the governor's amendments.
While an $80 million increase in income tax estimated payments collected by the state in January 1997, New York State expects to get that much less in April, the tax filing deadline.
